newsitem.title: FINLAND: FUND MANAGERS WELCOME IVO OFFERING, WANT LIQUIDITY.
newsitem.headline: FUND MANAGERS WELCOME IVO OFFERING, WANT LIQUIDITY.

text.p: Finnish electricity producer Imatran Voima will be an attractive addition to the Helsinki Stock Exchange and many Finnish funds are willing to participate in a likely offering next year, fund managers said on Thursday.
Apart from attractive pricing, funds will also look for evidence that a large enough chunk of stock will be floated so the share will be liquid enough, they said.
"There must be a clear indication from the government that a lot of shares will start moving, at least one third of the capital," said Arto Laukkonen at Selin Rahasto.
The government, which owns around 95 percent of IVO, said on Tuesday it would seek authorisation to lower its stake in IVO to below two-thirds.
Laukkonen noted that other partly privatised state companies are now liquid but that there were initial problems.
"That kind of a company should have a large ownership base to support its future," Laukkonen said, adding that restructing in the sector may require capital.

For instance, the government last year liberalised the energy market so that industrial power users are in principal free to buy electricity from any producer, regardless of which grid they are linked to.
This goes further, with the entire Nordic area opening up for competition between producers and grids.
But Imatran Voima will not be entirely without capital to start with.

In the process of deregulating the market and preparing the privatisation of IVO, the government, IVO and the industry's Pohjolan Voima (PVO) have agreed to merge IVO's and PVO national grids into one.
This is expected to give IVO fresh cash, although details of the arrangement have not yet been settled.
Nevertheless, IVO vice president Kalervo Nurmimaki told Reuters recently that IVO wants capital from the Initial Public Offering.
"We hope that there will also be a share issue," he said.
Fund managers said they have not always found the government's share offers attractively priced, saying sometimes the government has been more eager to raise funds for itself than for the companies.
"There are examples in history that (the government) has been too greedy," said Matti Rusanen at Gyllenberg Fund.
He said a good incentive to attract Finnish private investors to participate in an IPO would be to offer them bonus shares if they hold their stock for a year, as Neste did in an IPO last year.
That would also help liquidity to build up, he said.

Imatran Voima has produced solid results this decade -- last year's 1.13 billion markka profit before extraordinary items was 14 percent of net sales -- and fund managers said the company has a good image and seems well managed.
It has a strong market position in Finland, but its valuation will probably suffer from the lack of growth prospects, they said.
"From a Finnish perspective, energy production and distribution ... is where we have basic knowledge that gives a competitive advantage," said Selin's Laakkonen.

But he said the price to earnings ratio for Imatran Voima shares should be below the Helsinki bourse average -- which analysts say is currently in the region of 10 to 12 times projected 1996 earnings.

Lacking benchmarks in the sector in Finland, investors will be looking at European producers, primarily Swedish and Norwegian power companies; although they have significant water power generation while IVO's biggest resource are its nuclear reactors, analysts say.
